claims.text: Chemical vapor deposition at approximately 1000–1100 °C in an inert or reducing atmosphere can coat tungsten particles with a few atomic layers of graphene.
An optimized interlayer binder or optimization step will maintain the graphene coating's integrity during sintering.
The intervention will produce a conformal, ultrathin graphene interlayer that remains intact on tungsten particles during consolidation.
The intact graphene interlayer will bridge tungsten and copper at their interface.
The graphene interlayer will reduce phonon interfacial resistance or scattering at the tungsten–copper interface.
Reduced interfacial phonon resistance will enhance heat transport through the W–Cu composite.
Graphene is chemically inert under the relevant processing and service conditions.
The graphene layer's chemical inertness and thermal conductivity will help retain mechanical bonding in the W–Cu composite.
The graphene-modified W–Cu composite will have substantially higher overall thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable unmodified powder-metallurgy W–Cu composite.
The graphene-modified composite will maintain or enhance mechanical strength and durability relative to the unmodified control.
The graphene-modified composite will retain irradiation resistance under fusion-reactor joint neutron exposure.
The predicted benefits will hold under the high-heat-flux and neutron-irradiation conditions typical of fusion-reactor joints.
Adherence to the specified CVD temperature, atmosphere, and interlayer optimization is necessary to obtain robust bonding and the predicted improvement.
Deviations from the specified processing conditions may cause incomplete coating transfer or graphene degradation during sintering.
